context_blurb:
Bare ground does not stay bare. Fresh lava, rock left by a glacier, a burned forest or an abandoned field fills, stage by stage, with one community after another; a community is all the living things that share a place. Ecologists call this slow change ecological succession.

Primary succession begins where there is no soil at all: on new lava, bare rock or a new island. Secondary succession starts where a fire, logging or farming cleared the plants but left the soil, with its seeds, roots and nutrients, the chemical foods plants draw from the ground, so regrowth is much faster. So what decides the kind is whether any soil is left for plants to root in. Cold rock bared by a melting glacier starts primary succession too, so heat does not decide.

The first living things on bare rock, the pioneer species, are often lichens. A lichen has no roots and drinks rain, dew and damp air. Part of every lichen is a fungus, and the fungus gives off acids that eat away at the minerals of the rock's surface. Rain weathers granite too, but far more slowly. Loosened grains mix with dead lichens into a thin first soil, where mosses take hold.

Each stage of plants leaves deeper soil behind as it dies and rots, and that is what lets the next, bigger kind move in. Deeper soil holds the water and nutrients that the bigger roots of grasses, then shrubs, then trees need. Each stage casts more shade, not less.

No one lives long enough to watch a dune become a forest, so how do we know? In the 1890s Henry Chandler Cowles studied the dunes along Lake Michigan: beach grass by the water, then cottonwoods, then pines, then oaks farthest inland. The lake had built its dunes one after another, so the farthest were the oldest. Cowles read the bands as stages that every young dune passes through as it ages: a line in space was a line in time.

On abandoned farmland in North Carolina, horseweed, asters and broomsedge grass come first, and within a few decades pines stand over them, because in bright sun pines grow faster than oaks and hickories. But the pines' shade keeps young pines from growing beneath them, while hardwood seedlings can grow in that shade, ready to fill each gap as the old pines die at 80 to 120 years. Shade does the work, not poison.

A forest has layers, from tall trees through shrubs to plants on its floor, and each layer gives its own food and hiding places, so far more kinds of animals can find a living there than among mosses. The newcomers move in from the land around; they do not evolve on the spot. Mosses make food from sunlight just as trees do.

In May 1980 the eruption of Mount St. Helens laid waste to two kinds of ground. Where the blast only knocked the forest flat, plants were green again within months. On that quicker ground, plants and roots had lived through the blast, sheltered by late snow or living on as roots in the soil, so it grew back as in secondary succession. Nearby, flows of hot rock left metres of pumice that stayed hot for weeks and killed everything, so that ground began almost from nothing, as in primary succession. Even so, a lupine took root there within about a year.

Surtsey, a volcanic island that rose off Iceland from 1963, has been closed since 1965 to all but a few scientists, so that life must arrive unaided. Its lava cooled fast: lichens grew on it three years after the eruption ended. Still, two decades on, just ten or so plant species had settled. Then gulls arrived to breed. Gulls feed at sea, so their droppings carried nutrients from the sea, nitrogen and phosphorus, onto the bare lava, and plants crowded into their colony while the ground outside stayed bare.

In his 1916 book Plant Succession, Frederic Clements held that each climate's succession ends in one climax community, which then stays; to him a plant community was like a living body. Henry Gleason challenged him from 1917, and in 1926 called a plant community a coincidence rather than an organism. Most ecologists today see the climax as far less fixed than Clements thought, because fires, storms and floods keep knocking patches back to earlier stages. Yet succession is not random either: its stages follow real patterns.
